hero.question: PLACEHOLDER: what is really going on inside a brain with dementia?
hero.description: PLACEHOLDER: Answer six quick questions, then explore real brain data one donor at a time. About 45 minutes.

poll.heading: What do you think?
poll.framing: Six statements about dementia. Go with your gut. No feedback until you finish.

items.statement: Dementia is a disease of the brain
Dementia is a normal process of ageing
Dementia is another term for Alzheimer’s Disease
There are many different kinds of dementia
People who eat healthily and exercise are less likely to get dementia

poll.benchmarkSource: Benchmark: Hassan, Hicks, Tabet and Farina (2026), Aging & Mental Health — 1,371 young people aged 11 to 18 in England. PLACEHOLDER: the per-statement percentages still need checking against the paper’s results table.
poll.classCodeHint: Your teacher may give you a code, like BIOL-12. Working alone? Leave it blank.
poll.privacyLocal: Your answers stay on this device.
poll.privacyShared: Your six answers and class code go to the workshop organiser. No name. No email.
poll.resultCompare: The average teenager in the study got {{benchmarkMean}} right.
poll.resultGap: PLACEHOLDER: {{count}} of these six statements fooled most teenagers.

lab.heading: Pick a case to run
lab.intro: Five guided simulations. Each one asks you to predict, look, test and conclude.
lab.dotNote: 1 dot = 1 donor. The thick line is the median. The box shows the middle half of donors (the IQR).

cheats.title: Correlation is not causation
cheats.body: Two things moving together does not mean one causes the other.

cheats.title: Sample size
cheats.body: Check the n under each group. Few donors means a shaky pattern.

cheats.title: Confounders
cheats.body: Age, sex or genes could explain a difference too. Split the data and see if the pattern holds.

cheats.title: Post-mortem tissue
cheats.body: Each brain is measured once, after death. You never see one person change over time.

cheats.title: mRNA is not protein
cheats.body: More mRNA often means more protein, but not always.

lab.observeMatch: The median is {{trend}} in the last group than the first. That matches your prediction.
lab.observeMiss: The median is {{trend}} in the last group than the first. You predicted {{prediction}}. A wrong prediction is useful: it shows what to look at again.
lab.observeNoPrediction: The median is {{trend}} in the last group than the first.
lab.stressIntro: Groups can differ in more than disease stage. Pick a variable and split every group by it. Does the pattern survive?
lab.stressCountsHeading: How the donors fall across groups
lab.stressCountsNote: If one column is mostly one kind of donor, that variable is tangled up with the groups.
lab.snapshotBridge: Turn it into a {{prizeValue}} essay entry

rules: Write {{wordsMin}}–{{wordsMax}} words on any finding from the SEA-AD data on this site.

prize.builderHeading: Build your essay: claim, evidence, reasoning
prize.builderIntro: Four boxes. One for each part of a scientific argument. Your draft saves on this device only.

sections.label: Claim and biological system
sections.prompt: What did you find, in which cells, in one or two sentences?

sections.label: Data evidence from SEA-AD

sections.label: A-level biological mechanism
sections.prompt: Use what you know from A-level Biology to suggest why this might happen.

sections.label: Evaluation and limitations
sections.prompt: How far can this data support your claim?

levels: Describes the chart in general terms, with no numbers.
Quotes at least one median correctly, with its unit.
Quotes medians and spread for the groups compared, and the number of donors.
Uses medians, spread and sample size together to judge how strong the pattern is.
Names the cell type or gene.
Links the finding to one A-level idea.
Explains a plausible mechanism using A-level ideas accurately.
Weighs more than one mechanism and says what evidence would tell them apart.
States that the data has limits.
Explains how a confounder or the sample size affects the claim.
Adjusts the claim to fit the limits, and proposes a next test.

ucas.heading: UCAS and careers
ucas.intro: Nobody is born knowing how university applications work. Here is what people rarely say out loud.
ucas.statementIntro: Admissions tutors want to know what you did and what you learned. “I found it interesting” does not tell them.
ucas.weak: I did an online project about Alzheimer’s and found it interesting.
ucas.strong: Investigating single-nucleus transcriptomic data from the SEA-AD atlas, I analysed the selective vulnerability of SST inhibitory interneurons across Braak stages, developing skills in evaluating donor spread and confounding variables.
statementWhy: It names the data and the method.
It says exactly what was analysed.
It ends on a skill, not a feeling.
ucas.statementWarning: Do not copy this sentence. UCAS checks every application for matching text. Write about what you actually did, in your own words.
ucas.compHeading: Beyond medicine: what is computational biology?
comp: Biomedical research is not only lab coats and pipettes. A lot of it happens on a computer.
Computational biologists write code to find patterns in huge biological datasets, like the one on this site. The same skills power bioinformatics, health data science and AI in healthcare.
You can get there from biology, biochemistry, biomedical science, maths, computer science or physics. Entry requirements differ, so check each course on UCAS.
founder: PLACEHOLDER [GIULIO]: a short personal note. What you did not know at 17, and why research is a series of steps anyone can learn.

teachers.heading: For teachers
teachers.intro: A free 50-minute workshop on Alzheimer’s disease and gene expression for Year 12 and 13, built on real research data.
value: Runs in the browser on a school Chromebook. No accounts. Nothing to install.
Keeps working if the school Wi-Fi drops.
One lesson: poll, guided simulations, then solo exploring.
The essay prize is optional follow-up work.

topics: 3.6 Organisms respond to changes in their internal and external environments (nervous coordination, synapses)
Module 5: Communication, homeostasis and energy (neuronal communication)
Module 6: Genetics, evolution and ecosystems (manipulating genomes)

decoders.title: Dementia is the symptoms. Alzheimer’s is one cause.
decoders.body: Dementia means memory loss and confusion that get in the way of daily life. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of it.

decoders.title: Some brain cells are hit harder than others
decoders.body: The brain has many cell types. A disease can change some a lot and others barely at all. PLACEHOLDER: one sentence on what is known for Alzheimer’s disease, from a subject expert.

decoders.title: Reading genes, one cell at a time
decoders.body: Every cell has the same DNA, but each cell type switches on different genes. Counting the mRNA in one nucleus shows which genes are on, and what type of cell it is.
